title: Amino Acids and Proteins
description: The building blocks of life and how they assemble into functional proteins

concepts.title: Amino Acids
concepts.contentHtml:
An amino acid has four groups on the central α-carbon: an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen, and a variable side chain (R group) that determines identity and properties.

There are 20 standard amino acids encoded by the genetic code. Their R groups range from simple methyl (alanine) to aromatic rings (phenylalanine, tryptophan) to charged side chains (lysine +, aspartate −) to sulfur-containing (cysteine, methionine).

Amino acids are zwitterionic at physiological pH — the amino group is protonated (–NH₃⁺) and the carboxyl is deprotonated (–COO⁻). Each has a characteristic pKa and isoelectric point (pI) — the pH at which net charge is zero.

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds and Protein Levels
concepts.contentHtml:
Amino acids link via peptide bonds — a condensation reaction between the –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of the next, releasing water. The resulting –CO–NH– bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance, making it planar and unable to rotate freely.

Protein structure has four levels:
— Primary: sequence of amino acids (the peptide chain)
— Secondary: local regular folding — α-helix (hydrogen bonds within one chain) and β-sheet (hydrogen bonds between adjacent strands)
— Tertiary: full 3D fold of the polypeptide, stabilised by hydrophobic, ionic, H-bond, and disulfide interactions
— Quaternary: assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits (e.g., haemoglobin: 4 subunits)

concepts.title: Protein Denaturation and Folding
concepts.contentHtml:
Denaturation is the loss of a protein's native 3D structure without breaking peptide bonds — the primary sequence is preserved but function is lost. Causes: heat, pH extremes, organic solvents, detergents (SDS), urea, heavy metal ions.

Why heat denatures: increased thermal motion disrupts the weak non-covalent interactions (H-bonds, van der Waals, hydrophobic) that hold the fold together. Once the hydrophobic core is exposed, proteins aggregate irreversibly — cooked egg white is the classic example.

Protein folding is driven thermodynamically by the hydrophobic effect (burying non-polar side chains away from water) and fine-tuned by specific interactions. Chaperone proteins (e.g., HSP70) assist folding in vivo, preventing aggregation. Misfolding is linked to Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and prion diseases.

title: Enzymes
description: Biological catalysts — specificity, kinetics, and inhibition

concepts.title: How Enzymes Work
concepts.contentHtml:
Enzymes are protein (or occasionally RNA) catalysts that accelerate biological reactions by factors of 10⁶ to 10¹². They work by lowering the activation energy, not by changing the overall free energy of the reaction (ΔG° is unchanged — the equilibrium is unaffected; only the rate changes).

The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site — a specific pocket shaped to recognise the substrate via complementary shape, charge, and hydrogen bonding. Two classic models:

— Lock and key: rigid complementarity (substrate fits preformed active site)
— Induced fit (Koshland): the enzyme changes shape upon substrate binding, optimising the fit and orienting catalytic residues

Most evidence supports induced fit. Hexokinase closes around glucose, excluding water that would wastefully hydrolyse the phosphate.

concepts.title: Michaelis–Menten Kinetics
concepts.contentHtml:
Michaelis and Menten modelled enzyme kinetics with a simple scheme: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P.

The rate equation is:
v = V_max [S] / (K_m + [S])

— V_max: the maximum rate when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate
— K_m (Michaelis constant): the substrate concentration at which v = V_max/2. A lower K_m means higher affinity.
— The Lineweaver–Burk plot (double reciprocal: 1/v vs 1/[S]) linearises the hyperbolic curve, allowing graphical determination of V_max and K_m.

Real enzymes are more complex (cooperativity, multisubunit, allosteric), but Michaelis–Menten is the essential first model for any enzyme system.

concepts.title: Enzyme Inhibition
concepts.contentHtml:
Inhibitors reduce enzyme activity and are crucial in drug design.

Competitive inhibition: the inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. K_m appears increased (harder to saturate), V_max unchanged. Reversible and overcome by excess substrate. Example: statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase (cholesterol synthesis), resembling the substrate HMG-CoA.

Non-competitive inhibition: inhibitor binds at a site other than the active site (allosteric site), reducing V_max without affecting K_m. Cannot be overcome by excess substrate.

Irreversible inhibition: inhibitor forms a covalent bond with the active site, permanently disabling the enzyme. Example: aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX enzymes; nerve agents (sarin) irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase.

title: Metabolism: Glycolysis and the Krebs Cycle
description: How cells extract energy from glucose

concepts.title: Glycolysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Glycolysis splits one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate molecules (3C each) in 10 enzyme-catalysed steps in the cytoplasm. Net yield: 2 ATP (net; 2 invested, 4 produced) and 2 NADH.

Three irreversible (regulated) steps:
1. Hexokinase: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (traps glucose in cell)
2. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): fructose-6-P → fructose-1,6-bisP (the key regulatory enzyme)
3. Pyruvate kinase: phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate

PFK-1 is inhibited by high ATP (cell is energy-rich) and activated by AMP (energy-poor) and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate — a master hormonal signal that integrates insulin/glucagon signals. Glycolysis works under anaerobic conditions (useful in fast muscle; cancer cells even favour it when oxygen is present, the Warburg effect).

concepts.title: Pyruvate Dehydrogenase and Acetyl-CoA
concepts.contentHtml:
Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and is converted by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) — a massive multienzyme assembly — to acetyl-CoA (2C), releasing CO₂ and generating NADH.

Acetyl-CoA is the universal fuel currency: fats and amino acids also feed into the cycle as acetyl-CoA. The thioester bond in acetyl-CoA stores significant energy (~31 kJ/mol), driving the subsequent condensation reaction with oxaloacetate.

PDC is regulated by phosphorylation (inhibitory) and dephosphorylation (activating). High NADH/NAD⁺ and high acetyl-CoA inhibit PDC, preventing overflow of carbon into the cycle.

concepts.title: The Krebs (Citric Acid) Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) to give citrate (6C), which then passes through the remaining 7 reactions of the 8-step cycle back to oxaloacetate. Per turn of the cycle:

— 3 NADH (carry electrons to the electron transport chain)
— 1 FADH₂ (another electron carrier)
— 1 GTP (direct ATP equivalent)
— 2 CO₂ released (accounting for the 2 carbons from acetyl-CoA)

The cycle is amphibolic — both catabolic (breaking down fuels) and anabolic (providing carbon skeletons for biosynthesis: α-ketoglutarate → glutamate → other amino acids; succinyl-CoA → haem synthesis).

Key regulatory enzymes: citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase — all inhibited by high NADH and ATP.

title: DNA, RNA, and the Central Dogma
description: Nucleic acid structure, replication, transcription, and translation

concepts.title: DNA Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands. Each nucleotide has a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T).

The two strands are held by Watson–Crick base pairing: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds), G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds). G–C pairs are stronger — high G+C content raises the melting temperature of DNA.

The backbone (sugar–phosphate) is on the outside; bases are on the inside, stacked by hydrophobic interactions and van der Waals forces. The helix has a major groove and a minor groove — protein transcription factors and drugs bind these grooves to read or modify genetic information.

concepts.title: Replication and Transcription
concepts.contentHtml:
DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new double helix contains one old strand and one new. Key enzymes: helicase (unwinds), primase (lays RNA primer), DNA polymerase III (adds dNTPs 5'→3'), ligase (joins fragments). The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously (Okazaki fragments) because polymerase only works 5'→3'.

Transcription: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand 3'→5' and produces mRNA 5'→3'. RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine. Only select regions (genes) are transcribed, under control of promoters and transcription factors. mRNA then carries the code to ribosomes.

concepts.title: Translation and the Genetic Code
concepts.contentHtml:
Translation occurs at ribosomes. tRNA molecules carry specific amino acids and anticodons that pair with mRNA codons (3-nucleotide sequences). The ribosome moves along the mRNA, linking amino acids via peptide bonds to build a protein.

The genetic code: 4³ = 64 possible codons encode 20 amino acids → code is degenerate (most amino acids have multiple codons) and essentially universal (the same code in bacteria, yeast, and humans). Three codons are stop signals (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG is both the start codon and codes for methionine.

The order DNA → RNA → protein is the central dogma. Reverse transcriptase (in retroviruses like HIV) copies RNA back to DNA — the information can flow backwards.

title: Oxidative Phosphorylation and ATP Synthesis
description: The electron transport chain, chemiosmosis, and how cells make most of their ATP

concepts.title: The Electron Transport Chain
concepts.contentHtml:
The electron transport chain (ETC) is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons at Complex I and II respectively; electrons pass through complexes (I → CoQ → III → cytochrome c → IV → O₂). Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor, reduced to water at Complex IV.

As electrons flow downhill in redox potential, the energy released pumps protons (H⁺) across the inner membrane from matrix to intermembrane space at Complexes I, III, and IV — creating a proton-motive force (pmf) consisting of a pH gradient (ΔpH) and an electrical potential (ΔΨ).

Each NADH feeds ~10 protons; each FADH₂ feeds ~6 protons. This asymmetry explains why NADH yields more ATP than FADH₂.

concepts.title: ATP Synthase and Chemiosmosis
concepts.contentHtml:
ATP synthase (Complex V) is a molecular motor: protons flow back through its Fₒ subunit, down the electrochemical gradient, driving rotation of the γ-subunit within the F₁ head. Each 120° rotation of γ shifts the conformations of the β-subunits, converting ADP + Pᵢ → ATP. The three β-subunits alternate states (open, tight, loose) — Boyer's binding-change mechanism.

Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis (Nobel Prize 1978) explained that the proton gradient, not substrate-level phosphorylation, powers most ATP synthesis. From one glucose: glycolysis ~2 ATP, Krebs ~2 GTP, ETC ~26–28 ATP — total ~30–32 ATP per glucose (modern estimates replace the older '36–38' figure).

concepts.title: Uncouplers, Inhibitors, and Brown Fat
concepts.contentHtml:
Uncouplers short-circuit the proton gradient without generating ATP — protons leak back across the membrane, releasing energy as heat. Examples: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP, used as a dangerous weight-loss drug in the 1930s); thermogenin/UCP1 in brown adipose tissue (brown fat). Newborns and hibernating mammals use uncoupling to generate body heat.

ETC inhibitors block specific complexes:
— Rotenone: Complex I (used as a pesticide)
— Cyanide (CN⁻): Complex IV — blocks O₂ binding, halts the whole chain, fatal
— Oligomycin: ATP synthase — blocks the proton channel

Understanding these mechanisms explains the toxicity of cyanide and carbon monoxide (CO binds cytochrome c oxidase even more tightly than O₂) and informs drug design for metabolic diseases.

concepts.title: Lipid Bilayers
concepts.contentHtml:
Phospholipids have a polar head and two hydrophobic tails. In water they spontaneously form bilayers — heads facing the aqueous phases inside and out, tails sequestered in the middle.

The bilayer is a 5 nm-thick fluid membrane: lipids diffuse laterally (~µm/s) but rarely 'flip' across the membrane (slow, requires a flippase enzyme).

The fluid mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson 1972) describes membranes as 2D fluids of lipids with embedded protein 'mosaics.' Cholesterol modulates fluidity in animal cells.

concepts.title: Membrane Proteins
concepts.contentHtml:
Roughly a third of all proteins are membrane-embedded. They're hard to crystallize but essential — they include all transporters, most receptors, and many enzymes.

Transmembrane segments are typically α-helices (~20 hydrophobic residues spanning the bilayer). Some use β-barrels (mainly in bacterial outer membranes and porins).

Drug development heavily targets membrane proteins (G-protein-coupled receptors alone account for ~30% of approved drugs). Cryo-EM has dramatically expanded what's structurally accessible.

concepts.title: Lipid Diversity & Lipid Signaling
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond bulk membrane phospholipids, dozens of specialized lipids do specific jobs. Cholesterol (membrane modulator), sphingolipids (signaling), phosphoinositides (key regulators of cell trafficking), prostaglandins (inflammation signaling).

Lipid rafts — cholesterol/sphingolipid-enriched domains — concentrate signaling proteins. Lipidomics now profiles thousands of lipid species across cells and tissues.

Lipid metabolism dysfunctions underlie atherosclerosis, obesity, and many neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Signal Transduction
description: How cells detect and respond to signals

concepts.title: Receptors and Second Messengers
concepts.contentHtml:
A receptor protein detects a signaling molecule (hormone, neurotransmitter, growth factor). Binding triggers a conformational change that initiates a downstream signaling cascade.

Second messengers like cAMP, Ca²⁺, IP₃, and DAG amplify the signal inside the cell. One receptor can activate hundreds of enzymes.

The cascade allows sensitive detection (low concentration of signal still produces a strong response) and rapid termination (signal removed quickly).

concepts.title: GPCRs
concepts.contentHtml:
G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are the largest receptor family — hundreds of types in humans. Each has 7 transmembrane helices, binds a specific ligand outside, activates a heterotrimeric G-protein inside.

Activated G-proteins regulate downstream effectors like adenylate cyclase (making cAMP) or phospholipase C (making IP₃ and DAG).

About 30% of FDA-approved drugs target GPCRs. β-blockers, antihistamines, antipsychotics — all GPCR ligands. Lefkowitz and Kobilka shared the 2012 Nobel for GPCR mechanism.

concepts.title: Phosphorylation Cascades
concepts.contentHtml:
Many signaling pathways use kinases — enzymes that phosphorylate other proteins. Phosphorylation is the cell's most common reversible modification, controlling activity and localization of thousands of proteins.

The MAPK cascade, PI3K/AKT pathway, and JAK/STAT pathway are mainstays. Mutations in kinases drive many cancers — cancer-targeted kinase inhibitors (Gleevec, gefitinib, dozens more) exploit this.

Roughly 70 kinase inhibitors are FDA-approved for various cancers; an entire branch of pharma is built on this physiology.

concepts.title: Cofactors and Coenzymes
concepts.contentHtml:
Many enzymes require non-protein partners to function. Cofactors are typically metal ions (Zn, Mg, Fe). Coenzymes are organic molecules — many of which are vitamins or derivatives.

Examples: NAD+/NADH (from niacin) shuttles electrons in metabolism. Coenzyme A (from pantothenic acid) carries acyl groups. ATP (you've heard of) carries phosphate groups.

Without these helpers, the protein backbone alone can't do redox or group-transfer chemistry. Life depends on them.

concepts.title: Vitamins as Coenzyme Precursors
concepts.contentHtml:
Most vitamins are precursors to coenzymes that humans can't synthesize:

• Niacin (B3) → NAD+/NADH
• Riboflavin (B2) → FAD/FADH₂
• Thiamine (B1) → TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate)
• Pyridoxine (B6) → PLP (pyridoxal phosphate)
• Folate (B9) → tetrahydrofolate (one-carbon transfer)
• Cobalamin (B12) → methylcobalamin (rare reactions)
• Ascorbic acid (C) → cofactor for collagen hydroxylation

concepts.title: Deficiency Diseases
concepts.contentHtml:
Each vitamin deficiency manifests as a specific syndrome:

• Scurvy: C — collagen synthesis fails; bleeding gums, poor wound healing.
• Pellagra: niacin — diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia.
• Beriberi: thiamine — neurological / cardiac failure.
• Pernicious anemia: B12 — failure of red blood cell maturation.
• Rickets: D — bone mineralization fails in growing children.

Each was deadly until the responsible vitamin was identified — a major chapter of 20th-century medicine.
